- arrays, matrices, and maps are value-semantic headers over persistent
  storage;
- nominal structs are mutable reference values.

A non-`na` struct value denotes one storage identity. Assignment, arguments,
returns, tuples, fields, and collection elements copy that reference:

```tea
struct Point
    int x
    int y

Point p = Point.new(1, 2)
Point q = p
q.x := 3

// p.x and q.x are both 3.

q := Point.new(4, 5)
// q was rebound; p still denotes the first Point.
```

Every successful constructor evaluation creates a fresh identity. Tea exposes
no address, dereference, pointer arithmetic, or implicit struct-copy operation.
Physical stack, frame, or Heap placement is not source-observable.

Tea tuples remain compiler/runtime transport values: a tuple result must be
destructured at its declaration and cannot be stored under one source Name or
given independent history. Tuple elements carry their ordinary values, so a
struct element is a reference and a collection element is a header.

Drawing and table handles remain a separate external-resource domain.

## Structs

`struct Foo` is the canonical declaration spelling. Compatible block-form
`type Foo` declares the same fresh nominal `StructType`; `type Foo = Bar`
remains reserved for transparent alias syntax.

A constructor initializes the new struct's fields in canonical declaration
order while preserving source argument evaluation order. A field may contain
another struct reference or a collection header. Direct and mutual recursive
structs are finite because a struct field contains a nullable reference:

```tea
struct Node
    int value
    Node next = na
```

Field assignment evaluates and validates the receiver once before evaluating
the right-hand side, then transactionally stores the field through the
captured reference. If the right-hand side rebinds an ancestor Name, the
captured object remains the target.

Reading a field through a `na` struct reference returns that field's typed
empty value. Field mutation and mutable-method calls through `na` fail before
right-hand-side or explicit-argument effects execute.

Struct identity equality is not defined in this version. Use `na(value)` to
test for a null reference.

## Methods and shallow `const`

Methods are nested in their owning struct and have an implicit receiver named
`this`. The receiver is mutable unless the method has trailing `const`:

```tea
struct Counter
    int value

    int add(int amount) =>
        this.value := this.value + amount
        this.value

    int read() const =>
        this.value
```

A mutable method changes the referenced storage in place. It may be called on
any non-`na` struct-reference expression, including a reference returned from
a collection accessor or history read. There is no receiver copy-in/copy-out.

`const` is shallow: a const method cannot replace a direct field of `this`,
including a collection header stored there. It may mutate an independently
referenced child struct:

```tea
struct Parent
    int value
    Counter child
    array<int> samples

    void inspect() const =>
        this.value := 1       // rejected
        this.samples.push(1)  // rejected: replaces this.samples
        this.child.add(1)     // allowed: child is a separate reference
```

Bare `this` remains a non-escaping receiver capability in this version: it
cannot be stored, returned, passed, compared, dereferenced, or history-indexed.
Method parameter defaults remain caller-side declaration-scope expressions and
cannot reference `this` or another method parameter.

## Collections

Tea has these collection types:

- `array<T>`: a variable-length ordered sequence;
- `matrix<T>`: a fixed-shape rectangular row-major collection;
- `map<K, V>`: an insertion-ordered map whose keys are `int`, finite `float`,
  `bool`, `string`, `color`, or a nominal enum.

A collection value is a small immutable header. Assignment copies the header.
A mutator constructs replacement backing and stores a replacement header into
one writable location:

```tea
a = array.from(1)
b = a
b.push(2)

// a contains [1]; b contains [1, 2].
```

The sized array constructor may omit its initial value. Its declared element
type's empty value is used:

```tea
array.new<float>(3) // [na, na, na]
array.new<bool>(2)  // [false, false]
array.new<Point>(2) // [na, na]
```

A struct field stores a collection header by value:

```tea
struct Holder
    array<float> values

var a = array.new<float>(1)
var holder = Holder.new(a)

holder.values.set(0, close)
a.push(1.2)

// holder.values.size() remains 1; a.size() grows.
```

A collection whose element type is a struct stores references. Accessors return
ordinary element values, so a returned struct reference is mutable:

```tea
point = Point.new(1, 2)
points = array.from(point)
points.get(0).x := 9

// point.x is 9.
```

An accessor returning a collection header still returns an rvalue, so
`outer.get(0).push(v)` remains invalid. A collection field reached through a
struct reference is a location, so `points.get(0).samples.push(v)` is valid
when `samples` is a collection field.

A collection loop snapshots its complete input header at loop entry. Later
writes do not extend or reorder that iteration.

## History versions bindings

Every runtime variable uses the same bounded history semantics. `name[N]` reads
the value committed to that binding `N` iterations ago:

- primitive history contains prior primitive values;
- collection history contains prior headers and immutable backing;
- struct history contains prior references, never struct-body snapshots.

If a struct Name was not rebound, current and historical entries may contain
the same reference and therefore observe the same live body. If the Name was
rebound, history may contain a different, older reference. Mutating through a
historical struct reference is legal:

```tea
foo[1].x := 3
```

Historical collection headers preserve membership, not transitive struct
bodies. A historical `array<Point>` retains its old element references, while
the Points reached through those references remain live.

History syntax applies only to a direct readable binding. Computed-expression
history is rejected:

```tea
foo[1]             // valid
foo[1].x           // valid
foo.x[1]           // invalid
Point.new(1, 2)[1] // invalid
(high + low)[1]    // invalid
```

Bind the observation explicitly when its history is needed:

```tea
x = foo.x
oldX = x[1]
```

An offset must be a non-negative safe integer. Invalid or unavailable offsets
return the binding's declared empty value.

## Conditional evaluation and function return

Both `condition ? left : right` and block-form `if` evaluate the condition once
and execute only the selected branch. Both branches must still typecheck.

`return value` exits the enclosing function or method, including when nested in
loops, value-producing blocks, or a persistent initializer. Existing trailing
expression returns remain supported. A value-returning function must produce a
compatible value on every terminating path; a void function can use bare
`return`. The program entry runs to completion without a source return.
Returning from a helper never commits the runtime transaction independently.

## Named output writes

`emit "price" close` writes one named column for the current step;
`emit.append "fills" execution` appends a value to that column's list.
Names must be compile-time strings, including names forwarded through constant
function arguments. One name has one fixed Tea type and write mode. Duplicate
plain writers, possibly repeated plain writes in loops, and mixed modes are
compile-time errors. Multiple append sites may share a name and must agree on
its element type.

Emissions snapshot values immediately. Later mutation cannot change the emitted
value, and a failed step publishes nothing. Missing plain emission and an
explicit null both produce null; numeric `NaN` remains distinct. Append columns
start as empty lists and preserve runtime append order independently. Schema
column order is static declaration order.

## Transactions, realtime, `var`, and `varip`

One execution transaction owns tentative storage allocation, struct-field
mutation, same-row local candidates, frame activation, and buffered emissions.
An execution error aborts the transaction; successful execution commits it.

Local assignment records a pending write under that binding's identity. A later
read in the same attempt sees it immediately. The runtime opens calls lazily
and retains only changed local values in the write set, instead of building a
second mutable frame tree. Rollback discards those writes and buffered outputs;
accepted histories and intermediate values are replaced only after success.

Successful provisional ticks commit struct-body mutations. Consequently, a
shared reference supports natural realtime accumulation:

```tea
struct Counter
    int value

var counter = Counter.new(0)
counter.value := counter.value + 1
plot("output0", counter.value)
```

Successive ticks on one realtime bar observe `1`, then `2`, then `3`. If the
third tick fails after writing `3`, abort restores `2`, and retry starts from
`2`.

`var` and `varip` govern binding initialization and rebinding, not the body
reached through a reference. Aliases with different storage classes still see
one committed body. A first successful ordinary-`var` initialization on an
unconfirmed row retains an initialization-only same-row candidate so the
example also produces `1`, `2`, `3` on its first live row. Later ordinary-`var`
reassignments still roll back between ticks; `varip` retains them.

Persistent initialization occurs when execution first reaches the declaration,
not when its frame is allocated. Failure before a successful initializer commit
retains neither its value nor its initialized state.

## Runtime storage boundary

Within one runtime context, all source-hidden memory identities use the same
typed `Ref<V>` and Heap framework. Collection backing and generated class bodies
have different `TypeInfo<A, V>` policies over the same reference, transaction,
version guard, limits, reachability graph, and garbage collector.

In `Context`, the Heap is an owned execution resource, separate from committed
history and same-index values. `Context` owns and disposes the Heap and supplies
the active transaction to value operations. A successful step replaces its
state without transferring storage ownership to the caller.

Generated nominal structs are TypeScript classes with named captured-Value
fields and an erased unique-symbol brand. Their class constructor supplies
nominal identity and missing field values. Collection headers are frozen
generic classes, and their backing retains captured Values directly. There is
no parallel runtime structural type table.

Collection operations allocate persistent replacement backing. A struct field
write goes through the Heap transaction view and stages a replacement body for
the existing Ref. Transactional reads see pending writes, commit installs them,
and rollback discards them. The common transaction mechanism preserves class
prototypes and shared aliases; generated classes do not implement separate
transaction engines.

Output emission snapshots permitted struct fields at call time. It never hands
a live struct reference to an observer. Each request child owns an independent Heap,
and child request results are restricted to scalars copied by value into the
parent adapter. A `Ref` never crosses that boundary. For the Node-only
`security_lower_tf` path, a frozen scalar batch enters the parent step and is
materialized as an ordinary Tea array inside the parent Heap transaction. Detailed synchronization belongs to
[Requests](#requests).

## Empty values and errors

Tea keeps typed-empty semantics rather than Go zero initialization. `na`
collections and struct references are distinct from valid empty collections or
allocated structs. Bounds, shape, key, nominal-type, stale-reference, and configured storage-limit
failures use stable runtime error codes.

pages.title: Price and volume
pages.description: The current bar’s open, high, low, close and volume, and the averages built from them.
pages.intro:
Price and volume of the current row, read from input columns the host supplies.

Each name reads the input column of the same name, as [`close`](#close)
describes. The host must supply every column a script reads, or binding the
script fails. Library files can read these names too, and no file can
redeclare or assign them.

Available in every script without an import or namespace.

entries.summary: Opening price of the current row.
entries.body: Reads the host-supplied `open` column, like [`close`](#close).

entries.summary: Highest price of the current row.
entries.body: Reads the host-supplied `high` column, like [`close`](#close).

entries.summary: Lowest price of the current row.
entries.body: Reads the host-supplied `low` column, like [`close`](#close).

entries.summary: Closing price of the current row.
entries.body:
Reads the `close` column of the host's input stream. A row is one item of
that stream, such as one bar, and `close` is `na` on a row where the host
supplies `NaN`. Inside a [request](#requests) expression, it reads the
stream bound to that request instead.

`close[1]` is the value one row earlier and is `na` on the first row. This
computes the change from the previous row, using [`nz`](#nz) to treat the
missing first value as no change:

```tea
previous = nz(close[1], close)
emit "change" close - previous
```

entries.summary: Traded volume of the current row.
entries.body: Reads the host-supplied `volume` column, like [`close`](#close).

entries.summary: Midpoint of the current row's high and low, `(high + low) / 2`.
entries.body:
Tea does not compute it: it reads the host-supplied `hl2` column, like
[`close`](#close). `tea run` derives that column from `high` and `low` when the
CSV file lacks it.

entries.summary: Average of the current row's high, low and close, `(high + low + close) / 3`.
entries.body:
Tea does not compute it: it reads the host-supplied `hlc3` column, like
[`close`](#close). `tea run` derives that column from `high`, `low` and `close`
when the CSV file lacks it.

entries.summary: Average of the current row's open, high, low and close, `(open + high + low + close) / 4`.
entries.body:
Tea does not compute it: it reads the host-supplied `ohlc4` column, like
[`close`](#close). `tea run` derives that column from `open`, `high`, `low` and
`close` when the CSV file lacks it.

entries.summary: Average of the current row's high, low and doubled close, `(high + low + 2 * close) / 4`.
entries.body:
Tea does not compute it: it reads the host-supplied `hlcc4` column, like
[`close`](#close). `tea run` derives that column from `high`, `low` and `close`
when the CSV file lacks it.

pages.title: Bar and time
pages.description: The bar number, the bar’s time, the clock, and where the bar stands in the data.
pages.intro: Values the host supplies for the current bar, available in every script without an import.

entries.summary: The number of the current bar, counting from 0.
entries.body: It grows by one each time a bar is finalized; repeated updates of a live bar keep the same number. Inside a request expression it counts the requested data’s bars.

entries.summary: The current bar’s time, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch.
entries.body: It is the `time` field of the current input row, the time at which the bar opens. Reading it requires the bound data stream to carry that field; without it, the run stops with an error. Inside a request expression it is the requested data’s bar time.

entries.summary: The current clock time, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch.
entries.body: The host’s clock is read once for each execution, so repeated updates of a live bar can see different values. A host may supply a fixed clock instead, for reproducible runs. Inside a request expression it is read when the requested data’s bar executes.

entries.summary: Whether the current bar is the first one, where [`bar_index`](#bar_index) is 0.
entries.body: Inside a request expression it refers to the requested data’s first bar.

entries.summary: Whether the script is processing historical data.
entries.body: It is always the opposite of [`barstate.isrealtime`](#barstate.isrealtime), including inside a request expression.

entries.summary: Whether the script is processing live data.
entries.body: The host reports it for each execution. It is `false` unless the host marks the data as live, so runs over stored data report `false`. Inside a request expression it is read when the requested data’s bar executes.

entries.summary: Whether the current update is the bar’s final one.
entries.body:
It is `false` on provisional updates of a live bar and `true` on its final update. Rows that are not marked provisional are final, so historical bars are always confirmed. Inside a request expression it describes the requested data’s update. Use it to act only on completed bars.

**Example:**

```tea
var int completed = 0
if barstate.isconfirmed
    completed := completed + 1
emit "completed_bars" completed
```

**Output:**

```text
index  completed_bars
0      1
```

entries.summary: Whether this is the first update of the current bar.
entries.body: It is `true` for the first execution of each bar and `false` when a live bar is updated again. Historical bars run once, so they are always new. Inside a request expression it describes the requested data’s bar.

pages.title: input
pages.description: Script inputs a host can set without editing the source.
pages.intro: An input declares a value the host supplies when it binds the script, falling back to the default written in the source. [`input`](#input) explains how inputs are named and when their values are fixed.

commonParameters.name: title
commonParameters.description: The label a host shows for the input. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

commonParameters.name: tooltip
commonParameters.description: Help text a host shows with the input. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

commonParameters.name: inline
commonParameters.description: A host shows inputs that have the same `inline` text on one line. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

commonParameters.name: group
commonParameters.description: A host shows inputs that have the same `group` text together, under that text as a heading. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

commonParameters.name: confirm
commonParameters.description: When `true`, asks a host to have the user confirm the value before the script runs. Must be a compile-time constant.

commonParameters.name: display
commonParameters.description: Where a host shows the input’s value: `display.all`, `display.data_window`, `display.status_line` or `display.none`; other `display` constants are rejected. The default is `display.all` unless the entry says otherwise. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

commonParameters.name: active
commonParameters.description: Whether a host shows the input as enabled. It is evaluated when the script is bound and may read other inputs; it never changes the input’s value.

entries.summary: Declares a whole-number input.

parameters.name: defval
parameters.description: The value used when the host supplies none. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: minval
parameters.description: The smallest value the host may supply. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: maxval
parameters.description: The largest value the host may supply. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: step
parameters.description: The increment a host’s control uses between values. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: The only values the host may supply, as a bracketed list of distinct constants such as `[5, 10, 20]`; the default must be one of them.

entries.returns: The value the host supplied, or the default; it is the same on every bar.
entries.body:
Also accepts the common parameters `title`, `tooltip`, `inline`, `group`, `confirm`, `display`, `active`.

A value below `minval`, above `maxval` or missing from `options` is rejected when the host binds the script; `step` only guides a host’s control and is not enforced. The default must meet the same limits, `minval` cannot exceed `maxval`, and `step` must be greater than zero. `options` replaces the range arguments and cannot be combined with them. See [`input`](#input) for how inputs are named and when they are fixed.

```tea
emit "average" ta.sma(close, length)
```

```csv
1,11
2,10
3,12

6,10
7,15
```

```text

7      na
```

Tea does not check that the text is a valid timeframe. A common use is the `timeframe` of [`request.security`](#request.security).

pages.title: request
pages.description: Calculations evaluated in another symbol or timeframe.
pages.intro: A request evaluates an expression in a child context fed by its own data stream. [Request synchronization](#requests) explains binding and synchronization in depth.

entries.summary: Evaluates an expression on another symbol’s or timeframe’s data and returns its value for each bar.
signatures:
request.security(
    simple string symbol,
    simple string timeframe,
    series any value expression,
    simple string fill = …
)

parameters.name: symbol
parameters.description: The symbol of the requested data, recorded for the host, which binds the matching data stream. It must be known when the script is bound: a constant, an input, or a fixed value such as [`syminfo.tickerid`](#syminfo.tickerid). Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: timeframe
parameters.description: The timeframe of the requested data, such as `"60"` (60 minutes) or `"D"` (one day). Like `symbol`, it must be known when the script is bound. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The calculation to run on the requested data, with that data’s own bars and history. It must produce one `int`, `float`, `bool`, `string`, `color` or enum value. It may read the script’s constants and inputs, except source inputs, but no other script variables; call a function to use several statements. Evaluated in the requested context.

parameters.name: fill
parameters.description: What the result holds on a bar where no new requested value arrived since the previous bar: `"carry"`, the default, repeats the latest value, and `"sparse"` gives `na`. It must be known when the script is bound. Cannot be `na`.

entries.returns: The expression’s value from the requested data for the current bar, with the expression’s type; the type’s empty value (`na`, or `false` for `bool`) until the requested data has produced a value.
entries.body:
The call must be the entire initializer of a top-level variable, such as `daily = request.security(...)`. The host binds the requested data stream under that variable’s name; Tea fetches no data itself. When both data streams carry event times, each bar receives the newest requested value that opened at or before it; otherwise requested values are paired with bars in order. History inside `expression` refers to the requested data, so `close[1]` there is its previous bar. Inside `expression`, `syminfo` and `timeframe` values are what the host supplies for the requested data; Tea does not set them from `symbol` and `timeframe`. To get several values, declare one request for each. See [Requests](#requests) for binding and synchronization.

```tea
daily = request.security(syminfo.tickerid, "D", close[1])
emit "previous_daily_close" daily
```

entries.summary: Collects an expression’s values from finer-grained data into an array for each bar.
signatures:
request.security_lower_tf(
    simple string symbol,
    simple string timeframe,
    series any value expression
)

parameters.name: symbol
parameters.description: The symbol of the requested data, recorded for the host, which binds the matching data stream. It must be known when the script is bound: a constant, an input, or a fixed value such as [`syminfo.tickerid`](#syminfo.tickerid). Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: timeframe
parameters.description: The timeframe of the requested data, such as `"60"` (60 minutes) or `"D"` (one day). Like `symbol`, it must be known when the script is bound. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The calculation to run on the requested data, with that data’s own bars and history. It must produce one `int`, `float`, `bool`, `string`, `color` or enum value. It may read the script’s constants and inputs, except source inputs, but no other script variables; call a function to use several statements. Evaluated in the requested context.

entries.returns: An array of the expression’s values that belong to the current bar, oldest first; empty when there are none.
entries.body:
The call must be the entire initializer of a top-level variable, such as `ranges = request.security_lower_tf(...)`. The host binds the requested data stream under that variable’s name; Tea fetches no data itself. When both data streams carry event times, a bar collects the requested values that opened after the previous bar and up to its own time. Without event times, a bar collects a fixed number of values when both streams have regular periods that divide evenly, and one value otherwise. Inside `expression`, `syminfo` and `timeframe` values are what the host supplies for the requested data; Tea does not set them from `symbol` and `timeframe`. See [Requests](#requests).

```tea
ranges = request.security_lower_tf(syminfo.tickerid, "15", high - low)
emit "intraday_bars" ranges.size()
```

pages.title: Requests
pages.markdown:
Tea does not fetch requested data. An application supplies the root DataStream
and binds each request child by its declaration name. Node owns child execution,
synchronization, history, and cancellation.

## Write the calculation in its own input context

A request is a direct top-level declaration. Its captured expression runs on
the child's bars, with the child's own history. Use an ordinary function when
that calculation needs several statements:

```tea
previousAverage() =>
    average = ta.sma(close, 20)
    average[1]

daily = request.security("AAPL", "D", previousAverage(), fill="carry")
plot("previous_daily_average", daily)
```

Here `average[1]` means the previous **child** bar's average. `daily[1]` in the
parent would instead mean the value seen on the previous **parent** bar.
History indexing requires a named binding: bind a function result first,
then index it; `ta.sma(close, 20)[1]` is not valid Tea.

The request call itself cannot be inside a function, local block, method, or
another request capture. The function above contains only the calculation;
the top-level `daily` declaration owns the request. Symbol and timeframe must
be static: `simple` values such as constants, inputs and `syminfo.tickerid`.
Each capture returns one scalar. To obtain several values, declare
one named request per scalar; each declaration needs its own host binding,
even when their symbol and timeframe match. Tuple and struct captures are not
supported by the language checker.

The symbol and timeframe remain useful application-facing metadata in the
Program. They do not imply a registry, network client, or runtime
lookup. A browser, CLI, chart, or service decides how to turn that metadata into
a DataStream.

## Child execution

Each RequestEdge owns one recursive `Module` and one private child Node. The
child uses the same runtime rules as the root, but owns independent parameter
values and has no public outputs. `node.bind({length: 50}, ["daily"])` configures
the child named daily; `node.bind(stream, ["daily"])` connects its input. Both
return a new root Node and leave its previous tree unchanged. After each successful child step, Node copies the requested
scalar result into the synchronization buffer.

Only scalar results can cross the child boundary. Tuples, heap references,
resources, arrays, matrices, and maps are rejected by the language checker. Each
child owns and disposes its own runtime and Heap.

`request.security_lower_tf` still captures one scalar child result per child
index. Node groups those copied scalars and materializes the resulting Tea array
inside the parent Heap transaction.

## Bind streams by declaration name

```tea
daily = request.security("AAPL", "D", close)
lower = request.security_lower_tf("AAPL", "15", close)
```

The public binding key is the declaration name (`daily`, `lower`), never the
symbol. A root series and request with the same name are ambiguous and binding
fails before mutation.

```ts
batchRecipe(
  node,
  [parameters, rootStream, {daily: dailyStream, lower: lowerStream}],
  observer,
).execute();
```

Parameters and DataStreams remain the only `Node.bind()` forms. Request data is
not a third binding kind.

## Clock and event-time inputs

`DataStream.clock` describes a regular duration when known; `i` means irregular
or unknown. Event time is separate data, declared by ordinary Arrow fields:

```ts
import {Field, Float64, Schema, TimestampMillisecond} from 'apache-arrow';

const schema = new Schema([
  new Field('time', new TimestampMillisecond(), false),
  new Field('close', new Float64(), false),
]);
// {time: 0n, close: 10} opens at epoch millisecond 0.
```

These fields do not enter Tea numeric series. Timestamp values may be numbers
or bigints; Node requires exact safe epoch-ms integers in increasing order between
finalized steps. A non-nullable Bool `provisional` field enables repeated attempts
at the same timestamp; it defaults to false when absent. The current step must
finalize before time advances, and finalized timestamps cannot be revised.
Arrow `Int64` also supports existing bigint sources. Use non-nullable times for
timed request synchronization; nullable time fields can represent absent or
explicitly null event metadata.

## Synchronization policies

Node folds request edges in dense request-id order. The parent does not step
until every edge has supplied a value for the current parent input.

A child value is eligible for a parent input once the child's event time is at
or before the parent's event time. `request.security` uses one generic field:

- `fill="carry"` reuses the last eligible child value across later parent inputs,
  including when the child has no new observation. `fill="sparse"` leaves those
  gaps empty. For comparisons requiring matching observations, use sparse and
  preserve missing values; carry means "latest available", not "same time".

Tea intentionally does not expose Pine's `barmerge.gaps_*` or
`barmerge.lookahead_*` vocabulary, and it has no end-of-interval availability.
For a completed-interval calculation, select by the child's timestamp and the
host's interval boundaries. A child's `[1]` means its previous observation,
not necessarily its most recently completed interval: if no forming child row
is supplied, the latest child may already be complete. Test both input shapes.

| Request policy      | Required metadata                               | Parent value                                         |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| timed scalar        | `time` on both streams                          | newest child opened at or before the parent, filled  |
| scalar positional   | otherwise                                       | next child scalar                                    |
| event-time collect  | `time` on both streams                          | child opens between consecutive parent opens         |
| fixed-count collect | divisible known clocks and no usable event time | next `parentClock / childClock` child values         |
| positional collect  | otherwise                                       | next child scalar wrapped as a one-element Tea array |

Observed event boundaries outrank clock ratios because duration alone does not
prove phase alignment or the absence of missing observations.

An empty timed scalar child produces the result layout's typed empty value. An
empty timed collect window produces `[]`. Provisional parent attempts retain the
same child window; final parent attempts advance it. Multiple attempts of one
child step contribute only its latest value, never duplicate collect entries.
Positional final attempts wait for their child steps to finalize.

A new child step that arrives after its parent interval finalized is rejected
before that child step executes. Refinements of the current uncommitted child
step remain valid, even if its higher-timeframe open precedes the parent's last
time. They affect subsequent parent attempts only; child delivery alone does not
rerun a committed parent. Applications deliver known child changes before the
parent attempt that should use them. Future values remain buffered.

## Ordering, completion, errors, and cancellation

- Request children subscribe before their parent so cold finite sources can
  populate the synchronization buffer.
- A child error fails the shared Node graph once.
- A parent error or observer delivery error unsubscribes every child.
- Disposing the root Node recursively disposes all child runtimes.
- Timed synchronization may continue serving parent inputs after a finite child
  completes; carried scalar values and typed empty values do not require a live
  child subscription.

There is no request queue, source budget, context lease, or fixed result
column. Node retains only the buffered copied values required by the selected
policy.

## Static request metadata

Each module request entry retains the request declaration's symbol, timeframe,
mode, result layout, and synchronization policy. This is static language data,
not an instruction for Tea to acquire external data.
The application chooses how much history the child DataStream holds; Node
correctness depends only on the stream it actually receives.

## Staged beyond this slice

- dynamic requests;
- requests nested inside another request capture;
- live watermark policies;
- an application-specific source registry, if an application chooses to build
  one.

pages.title: Plots
pages.description: Lines, levels, fills, shapes, characters and colors a host draws, and their style constants.
pages.intro:
Each call writes one named output that a host can draw. See outputs and events.

Functions that describe plots, shapes, colors and alerts as named outputs.

Each call records its arguments in a description value and writes it to the
output named by its first argument, `id`. Tea draws and sends nothing: the
host decides how to draw or deliver each output, so options such as
`linewidth` or `display` are hints recorded exactly as passed. Only the
script itself can call these functions, not a library file.

An `id` is a constant string, unique among the script's outputs; only alert
calls may share one. It cannot be empty or one of `index`, `time`, `timed`
and `provisional`. Apart from the alerts, a call may run at most once per
row, so not inside a loop, and on a row where it does not run, such as
inside an `if` whose condition is false, its output holds no value.

Available in every script without an import or namespace.

entries.summary: Writes one value per row, with options for drawing it, to a named output.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the output this call writes.

parameters.name: series
parameters.description: Value to plot on the current row; may be `na`.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: Color on the current row, such as [`color.red`](#color.*); it may change from row to row. `na` records no color, leaving the choice to the host.

parameters.name: style
parameters.description: How to draw the values: a `plot.style_*` constant such as [`plot.style_line`](#plot.style_*), [`plot.style_histogram`](#plot.style_*) or [`plot.style_columns`](#plot.style_*).

parameters.name: trackprice
parameters.description: Whether to also mark the latest value with a horizontal price line.

parameters.name: histbase
parameters.description: Base level for the histogram, column and area styles.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of rows to shift the drawing by.

parameters.name: editable
parameters.description: Whether users may edit the output's style in the host.

parameters.name: show_last
parameters.description: How many of the most recent rows to draw.

parameters.name: display
parameters.description: Where the output appears: a `display.*` constant such as [`display.all`](#display.*) or [`display.none`](#display.*).

parameters.name: precision
parameters.description: Number of decimal places to show.

entries.returns: The description written to `id`. Its fields hold the arguments under the parameter names, such as `series` and `color`; pass it to [`fill`](#fill) to shade between two plots.
entries.body:
This plots a 20-row average, green while the close is above it:

```tea
average = ta.sma(close, 20)
plot("average", average, "SMA 20", color=close > average ? color.green : color.red, linewidth=2)
```

parameters.name: id

parameters.name: price
parameters.description: Level of the line. It can come from an input but cannot change from row to row.

parameters.name: color

entries.summary: Writes a shaded area between two plots or horizontal lines to a named output.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the output this call writes.

parameters.name: plot1
parameters.description: One edge of the area: the value returned by [`plot`](#plot) or [`hline`](#hline). Only its `id` is recorded.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: Fill color on the current row; it may change from row to row. `na` records no color, leaving the choice to the host.

parameters.name: editable
parameters.description: Whether users may edit the output's style in the host.

parameters.name: display
parameters.description: Where the output appears: a `display.*` constant such as [`display.all`](#display.*) or [`display.none`](#display.*).

entries.returns: The description written to `id`; its `first` and `second` fields hold the IDs of `plot1` and `plot2`.
entries.body:
The description refers to the two outputs by their IDs. This shades the area
between a fast and a slow average:

```tea
fast = plot("fast", ta.ema(close, 10), "Fast EMA", color=color.blue)
slow = plot("slow", ta.ema(close, 30), "Slow EMA", color=color.orange)
fill("band", fast, slow, color=color.new(color.blue, 80))
```

parameters.name: id

parameters.name: series

parameters.name: style

pages.title: Alerts
pages.description: Alert conditions and alert messages a host can deliver.
pages.intro:
Each call writes one named output that a host can deliver as an alert. See outputs and events.

Functions that describe plots, shapes, colors and alerts as named outputs.

Each call records its arguments in a description value and writes it to the
output named by its first argument, `id`. Tea draws and sends nothing: the
host decides how to draw or deliver each output, so options such as
`linewidth` or `display` are hints recorded exactly as passed. Only the
script itself can call these functions, not a library file.

An `id` is a constant string, unique among the script's outputs; only alert
calls may share one. It cannot be empty or one of `index`, `time`, `timed`
and `provisional`. Apart from the alerts, a call may run at most once per
row, so not inside a loop, and on a row where it does not run, such as
inside an `if` whose condition is false, its output holds no value.

Available in every script without an import or namespace.

entries.summary: Appends an alert event with fixed text on each row where a condition is true.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the event list this call appends to. Several `alertcondition` calls may share one `id`; their events keep the order in which the calls run.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Whether to append an event on the current row.

entries.returns: Nothing; use the call as a statement.
entries.body:
Each such row appends one event with the fields `title` and `message`; other
rows append nothing. A condition that stays true appends an event on every
row, so pass a transition such as [`ta.crossover`](#ta.crossover) to alert once per
crossing. When the host re-runs the current row with live updates, each run
replaces that row's events; combine the condition with
[`barstate.isconfirmed`](#barstate.isconfirmed) to append only on the row's final run. Tea
sends no notification: the host decides what to do with each event.

```tea
crossed = ta.crossover(close, ta.sma(close, 20))
alertcondition("cross", barstate.isconfirmed and crossed, "Cross", "Close crossed its 20-row average")
```

entries.summary: Appends an alert event with per-row text and a struct payload on each row where a condition is true.
signatures:
alert(
    const string id,
    series bool condition,
    series string title,
    series string message,
    data
)

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the event list this call appends to. Several `alert` calls may share one `id` when they pass the same `data` type; an `alertcondition` call cannot share it.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Whether to append an event on the current row.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Event title; may change from row to row.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Event message; may change from row to row.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Payload: any struct value, such as `Move.new(syminfo.ticker, close)`. Numbers, arrays and other non-struct values are rejected.

entries.returns: Nothing; use the call as a statement.
entries.body:
Each row where `condition` is true appends one event with the fields
`title`, `message` and `data`; other rows append nothing. Unlike
[`alertcondition`](#alertcondition), the text can change from row to row, and `data`
carries a struct value whose fields keep their types in the output. Repeated
true rows and live re-runs behave as for [`alertcondition`](#alertcondition).

```tea
struct Move
    string symbol
    float price

alert("move", barstate.isconfirmed and close > 50, "Price above 50", "Close " + str.tostring(close), Move.new(syminfo.ticker, close))
```

pages.title: ta
pages.description: Moving averages, oscillators, bands, crosses, pivots and volume indicators.
pages.intro:
Technical-analysis functions: moving averages, oscillators, volatility bands, crosses and running statistics.

Each written call keeps its own history and state, covering only the bars on
which that call runs. Call these functions on every bar and combine their
results with conditions afterwards: a call inside an `if` branch, one arm of a
ternary, or after `and` or `or` does not run when that code is skipped, so its
window reads the skipped bars as `na` and its running state does not change on
them. A call inside a loop shares one history and state across all iterations.
See values and control flow.

Most results are `na` until enough bars have arrived; each entry states when.
After that, a window function leaves out the `na` values in its window and is
`na` only when none is left. A few, such as [`ta.swma`](#ta.swma) and
[`ta.change`](#ta.change), say instead that an `na` value makes the result `na`.
The time-series guide covers warm-up and
crossing rules.

```tea
// Call on every bar, then combine the result with the condition.
risingThree = ta.rising(close, 3)
emit "signal" close > open and risingThree
```

Available in every script as `ta.name` without an import.

entries.summary: Simple moving average of the last `length` values of `source`.
entries.returns: The mean; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
Values that are `na` are left out: the mean is over the window's other
values.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{sma}_t = \frac{1}{|K_t|} \sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i},
\qquad K_t = \{\, i \in \{0, \dots, \mathit{length}-1\} : \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \mathrm{na} \,\}
$$

entries.summary: Exponential moving average of `source`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars; larger values react more slowly.

entries.returns: The average; `na` before the first value of `source`.
entries.body:
Each bar moves the average toward `source` by `2 / (length + 1)` of the
difference. It starts from the first value of `source` instead of waiting for
`length` bars, and a bar where `source` is `na` leaves it unchanged.
Compare [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma), which waits for `length` values.

entries.summary: Wilder's moving average of `source`, the smoothing behind [`ta.rsi`](#ta.rsi), [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr) and [`ta.dmi`](#ta.dmi).

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: The average; `na` until `length` values that are not `na` have arrived.
entries.body:
It starts as the simple average of the first `length` values that are not
`na`, then moves toward each new value by `1 / length` of the difference. An
`na` value is skipped: it does not count toward the first `length` values,
and later the previous result is kept.

entries.summary: Linearly weighted moving average of the last `length` values of `source`.
entries.returns: The weighted mean; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
The newest value has weight `length`, the one before it `length - 1`, and so
on down to `1` for the oldest. Values that are `na` are left out with their
weights.

entries.summary: Volume-weighted moving average of the last `length` values of `source`.
entries.returns: The weighted mean; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when the bars used have no volume.
entries.body:
It is the sum of `source * volume` divided by the sum of [`volume`](#volume), over
the window's bars where both are known.

entries.summary: Hull moving average of `source`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars, an `int` of at least `2`.

entries.returns: The average; `na` for the first `length + math.floor(math.sqrt(length)) - 2` bars.
entries.body:
It is the [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma) over `math.floor(math.sqrt(length))` bars of
`2 * ta.wma(source, length / 2) - ta.wma(source, length)`, with `length / 2`
rounded down. Like [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma), it leaves out `na` values.

entries.summary: Symmetrically weighted moving average of the last four values of `source`.
entries.returns: The weighted mean; `na` for the first three bars and while any of the four values is `na`.
entries.body:
The weights are `1/6`, `2/6`, `2/6` and `1/6`, from the oldest value to the
newest.

entries.summary: Arnaud Legoux moving average: a bell-curve-weighted average of the last `length` values of `source`.
signatures: ta.alma(source, int length, offset, sigma, bool floor = false)

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Position of the peak weight, from `0` (oldest value) to `1` (newest value).

parameters.name: sigma
parameters.description: Narrowness of the curve; larger values concentrate the weight near the peak.

parameters.name: floor
parameters.description: `true` rounds the peak position down to a whole bar.

entries.returns: The weighted mean; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and while any value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
The weights follow a Gaussian curve whose peak sits at `offset` across the
window and whose standard deviation is `length / sigma` bars.

entries.summary: Value of the least-squares line through the last `length` values of `source`, `offset` bars before the current bar.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars, an `int` of at least `2`.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Bars back from the current bar at which to read the line; `0` reads it at the current bar.

entries.returns: The line's value; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and while any value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
The line is fitted with the oldest value at position `0` and the current value
at position `length - 1`, then read at position `length - 1 - offset`. A
negative `offset` extends the line past the current bar.

entries.summary: Center of gravity of the last `length` values of `source`.
entries.returns: The center of gravity; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars, when every value in the window is `na`, and when the known values sum to `0`.
entries.body:
It is minus the sum of `source[i] * (i + 1)` divided by the sum of
`source[i]`, for `i` from `0` (the current bar) to `length - 1`, so it is
negative when the values are positive. Values that are `na` are left out.

entries.summary: Difference between `source` now and `length` bars ago.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars back, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: `source - source[length]`; `na` for the first `length` bars and when either value is `na`.

entries.summary: Momentum: `source` minus its value `length` bars ago.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars back, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: `source - source[length]`; `na` for the first `length` bars and when either value is `na`.
entries.body: It is the same as [`ta.change`](#ta.change), with `length` required.

entries.summary: Rate of change: the percentage change of `source` from `length` bars ago.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars back, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: `100 * (source - source[length]) / source[length]`; `na` for the first `length` bars, when either value is `na`, and when `source[length]` is `0`.

entries.summary: Relative strength index of `source`, from `0` to `100`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: The index; `na` for the first `length` bars.
entries.body:
Gains and losses from [`ta.change`](#ta.change) are each smoothed with
[`ta.rma`](#ta.rma) over `length` bars, and the result is
`100 - 100 / (1 + gain / loss)`. It is `100` when the smoothed loss is `0`,
including on a flat series, and `0` when the smoothed gain is `0`.

entries.summary: Chande momentum oscillator of `source`, from `-100` to `100`.
entries.returns: The oscillator; `na` for the first `length` bars, when no change in the window is known, and when `source` did not change over the window.
entries.body:
Over the last `length` bar-to-bar changes, it is
`100 * (gains - losses) / (gains + losses)`. A change that involves an `na`
value is left out.

entries.summary: True strength index of `source`, from `-1` to `1`.

parameters.name: short_length
parameters.description: Length of the second smoothing, in bars.

parameters.name: long_length
parameters.description: Length of the first smoothing, in bars.

entries.returns: The index; `na` on the first bar and until `source` has changed.
entries.body:
The bar-to-bar change of `source` is smoothed twice with [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema),
first over `long_length` bars and then over `short_length` bars, and divided
by the absolute change smoothed the same way.

entries.summary: Stochastic oscillator: where `source` sits between the lowest `l` and highest `h` of the last `length` bars.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Series to place in the range, usually [`close`](#close).

parameters.name: h
parameters.description: Series whose highest value is the top of the range, usually [`high`](#high).

parameters.name: l
parameters.description: Series whose lowest value is the bottom of the range, usually [`low`](#low).

entries.returns: The percentage; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars, when `source` is `na` or a window has no known value, and when the range is `0`. Values that are `na` are left out of the windows.
entries.body:
It is `100 * (source - lowest) / (highest - lowest)`, from `0` to `100` when
`source` lies within that range. The result is not smoothed; pass it to
[`ta.sma`](#ta.sma) to smooth it.

```tea
k = ta.sma(ta.stoch(close, high, low, 14), 3)
d = ta.sma(k, 3)
emit "k" k
emit "d" d
```

entries.summary: Commodity channel index of `source`.
entries.returns: The index; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars, when `source` is `na`, and when the known values in the window are all equal.
entries.body:
It is `(source - mean) / (0.015 * deviation)`, where `mean` is the
[`ta.sma`](#ta.sma) and `deviation` the [`ta.dev`](#ta.dev) of the last `length` values.
Values that are `na` are left out of both.

entries.summary: Williams %R: where [`close`](#close) sits within the range of the last `length` bars, from `-100` to `0`.
entries.returns: The percentage; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars, while any price in the window is `na`, and when the range is `0`.
entries.body:
It is `100 * (close - highest) / (highest - lowest)`, using the highest
[`high`](#high) and the lowest [`low`](#low) of the last `length` bars.

entries.summary: Money flow index of `source`, from `0` to `100`.
entries.returns: The index; `na` for the first `length` bars and when no bar in the window fell, and `0` when bars fell but none rose.
entries.body:
Money flow is `source * volume`, using [`volume`](#volume). Over the last `length`
bars, the flows of bars where `source` rose and of bars where it fell are
summed separately, and the result is `100 - 100 / (1 + rising / falling)`. A
bar whose change or flow involves an `na` value is left out.

entries.summary: Moving average convergence divergence of `source`, with its signal line and histogram.
signatures: ta.macd(source, int fastlen, int slowlen, int siglen)

parameters.name: fastlen
parameters.description: Length of the fast average, in bars.

parameters.name: slowlen
parameters.description: Length of the slow average, in bars.

parameters.name: siglen
parameters.description: Length of the signal line's average, in bars.

entries.returns: A tuple `[macdLine, signalLine, histogram]`, where `histogram` is `macdLine - signalLine`.
entries.body:
The MACD line is `ta.ema(source, fastLength) - ta.ema(source, slowLength)`,
the signal line is its [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema) over `signalLength` bars, and the
histogram is their difference. The averages start from the first value of
`source`, so all three are `0` on the first bar.

```tea
[macdLine, signalLine, histogram] = ta.macd(close, 12, 26, 9)
emit "macd" macdLine
emit "signal" signalLine
emit "histogram" histogram
```

entries.summary: Directional movement index: the +DI and -DI lines and the ADX trend strength, each from `0` to `100`.

parameters.name: diLength
parameters.description: Smoothing length for +DI and -DI, a positive `int`.

parameters.name: adxSmoothing
parameters.description: Smoothing length for ADX, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: A tuple `[plusDI, minusDI, adx]`. +DI and -DI are `na` for the first `diLength - 1` bars, and ADX for the first `diLength + adxSmoothing - 2` bars.
entries.body:
On each bar, the upward move of [`high`](#high) counts toward +DI and the
downward move of [`low`](#low) toward -DI, whichever is larger and positive.
Each is smoothed with [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma) over `diLength` bars and divided by the
true range ([`ta.tr`](#ta.tr)) smoothed the same way. ADX is `100` times the
[`ta.rma`](#ta.rma), over `adxSmoothing` bars, of the absolute difference between
+DI and -DI divided by their sum.

```tea
[plusDI, minusDI, adx] = ta.dmi(14, 14)
emit "+DI" plusDI
emit "-DI" minusDI
emit "ADX" adx
```

entries.summary: True range of the current bar.

parameters.name: handle_na
parameters.description: What to return when the previous [`close`](#close) is `na`, as on the first bar: `true` gives `high - low`, `false` gives `na`.

entries.returns: The true range, or the `handle_na` result when the previous close is `na`.
entries.body:
It is the largest of `high - low`, `math.abs(high - close[1])` and
`math.abs(low - close[1])`, using [`high`](#high), [`low`](#low) and
[`close`](#close).

entries.summary: Average true range: [`ta.tr`](#ta.tr) smoothed with [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma) over `length` bars.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: The average; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars.

entries.summary: Mean absolute deviation of the last `length` values of `source` from their average.
entries.returns: The deviation; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body: Values that are `na` are left out.

entries.summary: Variance of the last `length` values of `source`.

parameters.name: biased
parameters.description: `true` divides by `n` (population variance); `false` divides by `n - 1` (sample variance).

entries.returns: The variance; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars, when every value in the window is `na`, and for a sample variance of one value.
entries.body:
Values that are `na` are left out, so `n` below is the number of known values
in the window.

entries.summary: Standard deviation of the last `length` values of `source`.
entries.returns: The square root of [`ta.variance`](#ta.variance) with the same arguments; `na` whenever that is `na`.

entries.summary: Difference between the highest and lowest of the last `length` values of `source`.
entries.returns: The range; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body: Values that are `na` are left out.

entries.summary: Bollinger Bands: the average of `source` with bands `mult` standard deviations above and below it.
entries.returns: A tuple `[middle, upper, lower]`; each is `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and while any value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
The middle band is the [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma) of the last `length` values, and the
distance is `mult` times their population [`ta.stdev`](#ta.stdev).

```tea
[middle, upper, lower] = ta.bb(close, 20, 2.0)
emit "middle" middle
emit "upper" upper
emit "lower" lower
```

entries.summary: Bollinger Band width as a percentage of the middle band.
entries.returns: The width in percent; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars, while any value in the window is `na`, and when the middle band is `0`.
entries.body:
It is `(upper - lower) / middle * 100` for the bands [`ta.bb`](#ta.bb) returns
with the same arguments.

entries.summary: Keltner Channels: an exponential average of `source` with bands `mult` average ranges above and below it.
signatures: ta.kc(source, int length, mult, useTrueRange = true)

parameters.name: useTrueRange
parameters.description: `true` measures each bar's range with `ta.tr(false)`, so the range is `na` on the first bar; `false` uses `high - low`.

entries.returns: A tuple `[middle, upper, lower]`.
entries.body:
The middle line is `ta.ema(source, length)`. The distance is `mult` times the
[`ta.ema`](#ta.ema), over `length` bars, of each bar's [`ta.tr`](#ta.tr), or of
`high - low` when `useTrueRange` is `false`. The averages start on the first
bar, so there is no warm-up `na`.

```tea
[middle, upper, lower] = ta.kc(close, 20, 1.5)
emit "middle" middle
emit "upper" upper
emit "lower" lower
```

entries.summary: Keltner Channel width as a fraction of the middle line.
signatures: ta.kcw(source, int length, mult, useTrueRange = true)

parameters.name: useTrueRange
parameters.description: `true` measures each bar's range with [`ta.tr`](#ta.tr); `false` uses `high - low`.

entries.returns: The width as a ratio; `na` when the middle line is `0`.
entries.body:
It is `(upper - lower) / middle` for the channels [`ta.kc`](#ta.kc) returns with
the same arguments. Unlike [`ta.bbw`](#ta.bbw), it is not multiplied by `100`.

entries.summary: Supertrend: a trailing line on one side of price, and the trend direction.

parameters.name: factor
parameters.description: Band distance in average true ranges.

entries.returns: A tuple `[line, direction]`. `direction` is `-1` in an uptrend, where `line` is the lower band below price, and `1` in a downtrend, where `line` is the upper band above price; it is `1` until the ATR has a previous value. `line` is `0` on the first bar and `na` until the ATR has a value.
entries.body:
Bands sit `factor` times `ta.atr(atrPeriod)` above and below [`hl2`](#hl2).
The lower band never falls unless the previous [`close`](#close) was below it,
and the upper band never rises unless the previous close was above it. The
trend turns up when `close` rises above the upper band and turns down when
`close` falls below the lower band.

```tea
[line, direction] = ta.supertrend(3.0, 10)
emit "supertrend" line
emit "uptrend" direction == -1
```

entries.summary: Parabolic SAR: a trailing stop that moves faster toward price as the trend makes new extremes.

parameters.name: inc
parameters.description: Increase of the acceleration factor at each new extreme.

entries.returns: The level; `na` on the first bar, and on every bar if this call did not run on the bar where `bar_index` is `1`.
entries.body:
The trend starts on the bar where [`bar_index`](#bar_index) is `1`: upward with the
level at the previous [`low`](#low) if [`close`](#close) rose, otherwise downward
with the level at the previous [`high`](#high). Each bar the level moves toward
the trend's extreme price by the acceleration factor, which starts at `start`
and grows by `inc`, up to `max`, whenever the trend makes a new extreme. When
the bar's low falls below the level in an uptrend, or its high rises above it
in a downtrend, the trend reverses and the level jumps to the extreme of the
trend that ended. In an uptrend the level stays at or below the previous two
lows; in a downtrend, at or above the previous two highs.

entries.summary: True on the bar where `source1` moves above `source2`.
entries.returns: `true` on the crossing bar, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
It is `source1 > source2` on this bar and `source1 <= source2` on the
previous bar. Equality on the current bar is not a cross, and a comparison
with `na` is `false`, so the result is `false` on the first bar.

```tea
fast = ta.ema(close, 9)
slow = ta.ema(close, 21)
emit "crossedUp" ta.crossover(fast, slow)
emit "crossedLevel" ta.crossover(close, 100.0)
```

entries.summary: True on the bar where `source1` moves below `source2`.
entries.returns: `true` on the crossing bar, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
It is `source1 < source2` on this bar and `source1 >= source2` on the
previous bar. Equality on the current bar is not a cross, and the result is
`false` on the first bar.

entries.summary: True on the bar where `source1` crosses `source2` in either direction.
entries.returns: `true` when [`ta.crossover`](#ta.crossover) or [`ta.crossunder`](#ta.crossunder) is `true`, otherwise `false`.

entries.summary: True when `source` is greater than each of its previous `length` values.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of previous bars, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: `true` when `source` exceeds every known previous value, otherwise `false`; `false` for the first `length` bars.
entries.body:
Previous values that are `na` are left out; the result is `false` when
`source` is `na` or none of the previous values is known.

entries.summary: True when `source` is less than each of its previous `length` values.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of previous bars, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: `true` when `source` is below every known previous value, otherwise `false`; `false` for the first `length` bars.
entries.body:
Previous values that are `na` are left out; the result is `false` when
`source` is `na` or none of the previous values is known.

entries.summary: Number of bars since `condition` was last `true`.
entries.returns: `0` on a bar where `condition` is `true`, then `1`, `2` and so on; `na` until `condition` is first `true`.

entries.summary: Highest of the last `length` values of `source`, including the current one.
entries.returns: The highest value; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
Values that are `na` are left out. To compare against earlier bars only, read
the result's history:

```tea
upper = ta.highest(high, 20)
emit "breakout" close > upper[1]
```

entries.summary: Lowest of the last `length` values of `source`, including the current one.
entries.returns: The lowest value; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body: Values that are `na` are left out.

entries.summary: Bar offset of the highest of the last `length` values of `source`, as `0` or a negative number.
entries.returns: An `int` from `1 - length` to `0`; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
`0` is the current bar and `-1` the previous one; ties go to the most recent
bar. Values that are `na` are left out.

entries.summary: Bar offset of the lowest of the last `length` values of `source`, as `0` or a negative number.
entries.returns: An `int` from `1 - length` to `0`; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars and when every value in the window is `na`.
entries.body:
`0` is the current bar and `-1` the previous one; ties go to the most recent
bar. Values that are `na` are left out.

entries.summary: Value of a pivot high, reported `rightbars` bars after it, otherwise `na`.

parameters.name: leftbars
parameters.description: Number of bars before the pivot that must be lower.

parameters.name: rightbars
parameters.description: Number of bars after the pivot that must be lower; the pivot is reported this many bars late.

entries.returns: `source[rightbars]` on a bar that confirms a pivot high, otherwise `na`.
entries.body:
The value `rightbars` bars ago is a pivot high when it is strictly higher
than each of the `leftbars` values before it and the `rightbars` values after
it. Values that are `na`, including bars before the first, do not prevent a
pivot, so one can be reported with fewer than `leftbars` bars on its left.

```tea
pivot = ta.pivothigh(high, 5, 5)
emit "pivotHigh" pivot
emit "pivotBar" na(pivot) ? na : bar_index - 5 // bar index of the pivot itself
```

entries.summary: Value of a pivot low, reported `rightbars` bars after it, otherwise `na`.

parameters.name: leftbars
parameters.description: Number of bars before the pivot that must be higher.

parameters.name: rightbars
parameters.description: Number of bars after the pivot that must be higher; the pivot is reported this many bars late.

entries.returns: `source[rightbars]` on a bar that confirms a pivot low, otherwise `na`.
entries.body:
The value `rightbars` bars ago is a pivot low when it is strictly lower than
each of the `leftbars` values before it and the `rightbars` values after it.
Values that are `na`, including bars before the first, do not prevent a
pivot, so one can be reported with fewer than `leftbars` bars on its left.

entries.summary: Running total of `source` since the first bar.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Series to add up, such as [`volume`](#volume).

entries.returns: The sum so far; `na` before the first value of `source`.
entries.body: Values that are `na` are left out: the total keeps its value on those bars.

entries.summary: Highest value of `source` seen so far.
entries.returns: The running maximum; `na` before the first value of `source`.
entries.body: Values that are `na` are left out: the result keeps its value on those bars.

entries.summary: Lowest value of `source` seen so far.
entries.returns: The running minimum; `na` before the first value of `source`.
entries.body: Values that are `na` are left out: the result keeps its value on those bars.

entries.summary: Correlation coefficient of the last `length` values of `source1` and `source2`, from `-1` to `1`.
entries.returns: Pearson's correlation; `na` for the first `length - 1` bars, when no bar in the window has both values, and when either series is constant over the bars used.
entries.body: Bars where either value is `na` are left out.

entries.summary: Percentage of the previous `length` values of `source` that are less than or equal to its current value.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of previous bars, a positive `int`.

entries.returns: A percentage from `0` to `100`; `na` for the first `length` bars and while `source` or any of the previous `length` values is `na`.
entries.body: The result is `100 * count / length`.

entries.summary: On-balance volume: the running total of [`volume`](#volume), added on bars where [`close`](#close) rose and subtracted on bars where it fell.
entries.body:
It is `ta.cum(math.sign(ta.change(close)) * volume)`, computed once per bar
for the whole script.

entries.summary: Accumulation/distribution: the running total of each bar's volume, weighted by where [`close`](#close) sits between [`low`](#low) and [`high`](#high).
entries.body:
Each bar adds `(2 * close - low - high) / (high - low) * volume`, or `0` when
`high` equals `low`.

entries.summary: Price-volume trend: the running total of each bar's [`volume`](#volume), weighted by the relative change of [`close`](#close).
entries.body: It is `ta.cum(ta.change(close) / close[1] * volume)`.

entries.summary: Intraday intensity index of the current bar: where [`close`](#close) sits between [`low`](#low) and [`high`](#high), times [`volume`](#volume).
entries.body:
It is `(2 * close - high - low) / (high - low) * volume`; `na` when `high`
equals `low`.

entries.summary: Williams variable accumulation/distribution of the current bar.
entries.body:
It is `(close - open) / (high - low) * volume`; `na` when `high` equals
`low`.

entries.summary: Williams accumulation/distribution: the running total of each bar's move from its true low on an up bar, or from its true high on a down bar.
entries.body:
The true low is the lower of [`low`](#low) and the previous [`close`](#close); the
true high is the higher of [`high`](#high) and the previous close. A bar where
`close` did not change adds `0`.

entries.summary: Negative volume index: starts at `1` and moves with [`close`](#close), by its relative change, only on bars whose [`volume`](#volume) fell from the previous bar.
Positive volume index: starts at `1` and moves with [`close`](#close), by its relative change, only on bars whose [`volume`](#volume) rose from the previous bar.

pages.title: Core functions
pages.description: Missing values, conversions, script declarations and script errors.
pages.intro: Functions available in every script without an import.

entries.summary: Declares a file as a library and names it.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: The library’s name, which importing scripts use as its namespace. It must be an identifier: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit, and not a keyword. Must be a compile-time constant.

entries.body:
It must be the file’s first statement and appear only once. A script that imports the file uses this name unless it renames the import with `as`. See [Imports](#imports).

```tea
library("bands")

export upper(float source, float width) => source + width
```

entries.summary: Declares the script’s title and whether a host draws it over the price chart.
signatures: void indicator(const string title, const bool overlay = …)

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: The name a host shows for the script. It cannot be empty. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: overlay
parameters.description: `true` to draw the script’s outputs over the price chart; `false`, the default, to draw them in a separate pane. Must be a compile-time constant.

entries.body:
It must be the script’s first statement and appear at most once, and a library cannot declare it. The header only informs the host; it never changes how the script runs.

**Example:**

```tea
indicator("Bar range", overlay = false)
plot("range", high - low, "Range")
```

```csv
time,high,low
0,10,8
1,12,9
2,11,7
3,13,9
4,12,8
5,15,10
6,14,9
7,16,11
```

```text
1      {"id":"range","series":3,"title":"Range","color":null,"linewidth":1,"style":"line","trackprice":false,"histbase":0,"offset":0,"editable":true,"show_last":0,"display":"all","format":"inherit","precision":0}
```

entries.summary: Tests whether a value is missing.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: The value to test. It can have any type except `bool`, which is never missing.

entries.returns: `true` when `x` is `na`, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
Every comparison involving a missing value is `false`, even `!=`, and `x == na` is a compile error, so test with `na(x)`. Arithmetic without a defined result, such as division by zero or the square root of a negative number, gives `na`. An `na` array, matrix or map is no collection at all, unlike an empty one, and an `na` struct refers to no struct.

**Example:**

```tea
previous = close[1]
emit "has_previous" not na(previous) // false on the first bar
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,11
2,10
3,12
4,9
5,14
6,10
7,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  has_previous
0      false
1      true
2      true
3      true
4      true
5      true
6      true
7      true
```

entries.summary: Replaces a missing value with a fallback.
signatures: int nz(series int source, series int replacement = …)
float nz(series float source, series float replacement = …)
color nz(series color source, series color replacement = …)

parameters.name: source
parameters.type: series int, series float, series color

parameters.name: replacement
parameters.type: series int, series float, series color
parameters.description: The value to use when `source` is `na`. Without it, the fallback is `0` for numbers and fully transparent black for colors.

entries.returns: `source` when it is not `na`, otherwise the replacement.
entries.body:
**Example:**

```tea
change = close - close[1]
emit "change" nz(change) // 0 on the first bar
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,11
2,10
3,12
4,9
5,14
6,10
7,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  change
0      0
1      2
2      -1
3      2
4      -3
5      5
6      -4
7      5
```

entries.summary: Converts a number to an integer by dropping its fractional part.
entries.returns: `x` truncated toward zero, so `int(-2.7)` is `-2`; `na` when `x` is `na`.

entries.summary: Converts a number to a `float`.
entries.returns: `x` as a `float`; `na` when `x` is `na`.
entries.body: `float(na)` is a missing value of type `float`. Use it where a bare `na` has no type, such as a request expression.

entries.summary: Converts a value to text.
signatures: string str.tostring(series scalar | enum | resource value)
entries.returns: The text form of `value`; `"NaN"` when `value` is `na`.
entries.body:
Numbers use the shortest form that reads back as the same number: `3.0` gives `"3"`, `0.1 + 0.2` gives `"0.30000000000000004"`, and very large or small numbers use exponent notation such as `"1e+21"`. There is no format argument; round with [`math.round`](#math.round) first to limit the decimals. A `bool` gives `"true"` or `"false"`, a color its hex code such as `"#FF5252"` (with two more digits when it is transparent), and an enum member its title, or its name when it has no title.

**Example:**

```tea
emit "label" "Close: " + str.tostring(math.round(close, 2))
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,11
2,10
3,12
4,9
5,14
6,10
7,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  label
0      Close: 9
1      Close: 11
2      Close: 10
3      Close: 12
4      Close: 9
5      Close: 14
6      Close: 10
7      Close: 15
```

entries.summary: Stops the script with an error message.
entries.body:
When a call runs, the run stops: no output is published for that bar or any later one, and the host receives the message. When the conditions around a call are all constants that make it run, it is a compile error at the call instead, so `ta.sma(close, 0)` is rejected where it is written. A call inside a loop, inside a `switch`, or after a statement that can leave the block early is only checked when it runs.

This script stops on its first bar when the host sets `length` below 2:

```tea
length = input.int(14)
if length < 2
    runtime.error("length must be at least 2")
emit "average" ta.sma(close, length)
```

pages.title: math
pages.description: Arithmetic helpers and mathematical constants.
pages.intro: Functions and constants in the `math` namespace.

entries.summary: Returns the absolute value of a number.
entries.returns: `number` without its sign, with the same type; `na` when it is `na`.

entries.summary: Returns the sign of a number as -1, 0 or 1.
entries.returns: `-1` for a negative number, `1` for a positive one and `0` for zero, with the type of `number`; `na` when it is `na`.

entries.summary: Rounds a number down to an integer.
entries.returns: The largest integer that is not greater than `number`; `na` when it is `na`.

entries.summary: Rounds a number up to an integer.
entries.returns: The smallest integer that is not less than `number`; `na` when it is `na`.

entries.summary: Rounds a number to the nearest integer, or to a number of decimal places.
signatures:
float math.round(
    series int | float number,
    series int precision
)

parameters.name: precision
parameters.description: How many decimal places to keep. A negative value rounds to tens, hundreds and so on.

pages.intro: See [types](#reference/language/types) for the `array<T>` type and [memory model](#memory-model) for how array values are copied and shared. Unlike Pine Script, where collections are references, a Tea collection is a value: assigning it or passing it to a function copies it, so a function that pushes to its argument leaves the caller’s collection unchanged. Every function whose first parameter is `self` can also be called as a method on the collection: `values.push(x)` is the same call as `array.push(values, x)`.

pages.title: trade
pages.description: Coordinators that run a strategy's orders through a broker and record the fills in a portfolio.
pages.intro:
Coordinators that run a strategy's orders through a broker and record the fills in a portfolio.

Add `import trade` together with `import broker` and `import portfolio`. A
coordinator owns one broker value and one portfolio value: it submits your
orders to the broker, applies each fill to the portfolio, and refreshes the
account the broker checks before matching continues. Pick the family that
matches how your orders should fill: [`trade.nextOpen`](#trade.nextOpen) (next open, or
this bar's close), [`trade.ohlc`](#trade.ohlc) (anywhere in the bar's range),
[`trade.path`](#trade.path) (along an ordered intrabar path, with trailing exits) or
[`trade.lots`](#trade.lots) (separate lots, executed immediately). The broker
from [`broker.new`](#broker.new) holds one pending order and one attached exit at a
time. Store the coordinator in a `var` so its state persists across bars.
The strategy model describes each lifecycle in detail.

```tea
import broker
import portfolio
import trade

fast = ta.ema(close, 10)
slow = ta.ema(close, 30)
crossedUp = ta.crossover(fast, slow)
crossedDown = ta.crossunder(fast, slow)

var strat = trade.nextOpen(broker.new(), portfolio.new(initialCash = 10000.0))
strat.begin_bar(open, bar_index)
if crossedUp and strat.position_quantity() == 0.0
    strat.entry("Long", trade.Direction.long)
if crossedDown and strat.position_quantity() > 0.0
    strat.close("Exit")
```
